# Lockset

Guidance for agents working in this repository. Lockset gives repository secrets
a small, boring surface: per-principal grants on top of sops and age. It is a
CLI and a Rust library; there is no server and no second secret store.

Where this section differs from the shared Playbook rules, this section wins.
The deviations are deliberate and named with the rule they override.

## Workspace

- `lockset-core` — the model: `.sops.yaml` parse and rewrite, payload metadata,
  plans, and reports. No I/O, no environment, no OS code.
- `lockset-tools` — the adapters: `FsRepo`, `SopsCodec`, and custody over the
  OS keychain, `LOCKSET_AGE_KEY`, a file, or memory.
- `lockset` — the CLI and the orchestration as a library. `lockset::run` takes
  the parsed arguments plus `Inputs`; `main` is parse → run → exit code.
- `fuzz/` — libFuzzer targets for the input-heavy parsers.
- `scripts/` — the CI install, export, container, and artifact helpers.
- `confluence-docs/` — the local review and publish bundle for the Confluence
  space **LS — Lockset** (`spaceId` 171638788). It is not part of the build.

## Architecture invariants

- **`lockset-core` never does I/O.** No process spawn, filesystem, environment,
  or OS checks. Every external capability is a port (`Codec`, `Custody`,
  `Repo`) implemented in `lockset-tools`; the CLI injects the environment as
  `Inputs`.
- **Plans are data.** A command builds a `Plan` of `Change` values; the CLI
  renders it (`--dry-run`) or hands it to `exec::apply`, the only place that
  mutates anything.
- **Errors carry an exit class.** A `lockset_core::Error` variant maps to the
  exit codes in `README.md` through `usage::exit_code`. A new failure needs a
  class, not a bare `anyhow` string, unless it is a genuine runtime failure
  (exit 1).
- **No secret in argv or a file.** The identity reaches external tools through
  the child environment only; values are never written to disk; sops output is
  redacted before it is formatted.
- **Paths and rewrites are conservative.** `PathId` accepts both separators and
  refuses absolute, traversing, or ambiguous forms; rewrites touch only the
  lines they must and preserve line endings.

## Toolchain and gates

- `mise install` provides the pinned rust (1.99.1), `sops` (3.13.3), and `age`
  (1.3.2). The workspace MSRV is 1.89 and every dependency must build with it.
- Run repository tasks through `mise run`; a missing task is a gap to add to
  `mise.toml`, not a bare command to ship.
- `mise run check` is the full local gate: tests, lint (format, clippy, rustdoc),
  end-to-end, `cargo-deny`, and `cargo-audit`.
- `mise run e2e` runs the real pinned `sops` and `age`; `mise run fuzz` sweeps
  the parsers and needs the nightly toolchain and `cargo-fuzz`.
- CI runs the same versions from `mise.toml` on GitHub-hosted runners. The
  shared Playbook rule that puts every job on Blacksmith does not apply to this
  repository: it has no Blacksmith app, and the workflows use the GitHub-hosted
  `ubuntu-24.04`, `macos-15`, and `windows-2022` images.
- This repository has no TypeScript, no database, and no Sentry integration.
  The shared rules for those areas do not apply.

## Changing behaviour

- **New config field:** parse and validate it in `lockset-core/src/config.rs`
  with an error that names the field, resolve precedence in
  `lockset/src/wiring.rs`, document it in the README configuration reference,
  and test the default, the override, and an invalid value.
- **New command or flag:** add it to `cli.rs`, the dispatcher and handler in
  `app.rs`, the help and exit-code contract, and the README. Tests cover the
  plain path, the failure, and `--json` where a document applies.
- **New parser input:** add a proptest property in
  `lockset-core/tests/parsers.rs` and, if it parses untrusted text, a fuzz
  target in `fuzz/`.
- **Security boundary:** pin it in `lockset/tests/sops_contract.rs` (argv and
  environment) or the relevant contract test.

## Tests

- `lockset/tests/` runs the real binary against temporary repositories. Tests
  that need `sh`, permissions, or symlinks are gated `#![cfg(unix)]`; the
  shim-free tests must keep working on Windows.
- Shims (`LOCKSET_SOPS` pointing at a script) cover sops interactions
  deterministically. `lockset/tests/sops_contract.rs` records argv and
  environment and is the place to pin a security boundary.
- A new test must fail when the behaviour regresses, not just call the code. It
  must be deterministic and safe under `--test-threads`.

## Tickets

- Work is tracked in Jira at `yazee.atlassian.net`, project key `LS`, under an
  epic. Use the shared `jira-tickets` skill for the templates and the board
  workflow.
- Title it `[<AREA>] <description>`. Area tags in use: `[CLI]`, `[CORE]`,
  `[TOOLS]`, `[SECURITY]`, `[RELEASE]`, `[CI]`, `[DOCS]`, `[TOOLING]`.
- The board has `To Do`, `In Progress`, `In Review`, and `Done`. Move the ticket
  to `In Progress` when the branch is cut and `Done` after the merge.

## Lockset branches, commits, and pull requests

This repository's format overrides the shared git rule.

- One ticket per branch. The branch is named `LS-<n>` and is cut from the
  previous ticket's branch; the repository uses stacked pull requests, so the
  pull request targets that previous branch.
- Commit subject: `<type>(<scope>): <summary> (LS-<n>)`, for example
  `fix(run): keep the child's signal (LS-22)`. Types in use: `feat`, `fix`,
  `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `ci`, `chore`.
- Pull request title: the ticket title followed by the key, for example
  `[CLI] Add export for multi-step pipelines (LS-20)`.
- Never merge a pull request and never enable auto-merge. Open it, report the
  URL, and stop.

## Lockset releases

This repository's release flow overrides the shared `release.json` rule; there
is no `release.json` here.

- `cargo release patch --execute` (or `minor`/`major`) bumps every crate, opens
  the next `CHANGELOG.md` section from `Unreleased`, commits, tags `v<version>`,
  and pushes. The tag drives cargo-dist, the container image, and the action.
- Keep `Unreleased` accurate: it is the release body, and CI checks that the
  version's notes document the breaking change.
- The verification tasks are `mise run release:plan`, `release:build`, and
  `release:verify`. Crates publish in order: `lockset-core`, `lockset-tools`,
  `lockset`.

## Documentation

- The repository keeps what a deploy or a contributor needs: `README.md`
  (install, configure, operate), `SECURITY.md` (threat model and reporting),
  `CONTRIBUTING.md` (development and architecture rules), `CHANGELOG.md`
  (release notes), and rustdoc.
- The business and technical overview lives in the Confluence space **LS —
  Lockset**. Address the space by key. Publish page writes through the
  Atlassian MCP server and verify them with `acli`.
- `confluence-docs/` is the local, reviewable copy of that space; keep it in
  step when a documented contract changes, but do not treat it as build input.

## Generated output

- `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` are generated by APM. Never edit them by
  hand; edit `.apm/instructions/` or the Playbook package.
- `Cargo.lock` is committed and updated by Cargo, never by hand; build caches
  and `target/` stay out of the tree.

## Agent context

- The shared source is `Yazee-Me/Playbook`, pinned in `apm.yml`.
  `apm.lock.yaml` records the resolved commit and the content hashes.
- `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` are generated. Never edit them by hand;
  edit `.apm/instructions/` or Playbook.
- `apm.yml` targets `opencode`, whose output is exactly `AGENTS.md` plus
  `.agents/skills/` — the same surface every harness reads, so no per-client
  directory carries context. `.opencode/` stays empty until an agent or prompt
  primitive is added.
- A fresh clone or worktree has no `apm_modules/`. Run `apm install --frozen`
  before `apm compile`; otherwise compile omits the shared Playbook
  instructions.
- `mise run agent:sync` resolves the package and regenerates the context files.
- `mise run agent:check` verifies the committed output against the lockfile and
  Playbook, then runs `apm audit --ci`. Run it before a commit or pull request.
- `mise run agent:latest` compares the pin with the newest Playbook tag;
  `mise run agent:upgrade [version]` moves the pin and regenerates the context.
- `apm_modules/` is generated and gitignored.

## Shared ticket rules

- File the Jira ticket before the first edit. Every unit of work that lands as
  one PR is an issue first; never file it afterwards as a record of what
  happened.
- Title it `[<AREA>] <description>`. The project's instructions define the
  project key, site, and area tags. Keep the title inside 72 characters with the
  key and commit prefix in front of it.
- Every Story, Task, and Bug sits under an Epic. Create the Epic first when none
  covers the work; a Subtask inherits its parent's Epic.
- One ticket per unit of work. Do not stretch an existing ticket to cover an
  unrelated change. When the user names a key that already covers the work, use
  that key instead of filing a duplicate.
- The ticket title is the source of truth for the branch, commit subject, and PR
  title. Do not invent a second name for the same work.
- Move the ticket as the work moves: `In Progress` when the branch is cut, the
  review state when the PR opens, `Done` only after the merge. Take transition
  ids from `acli` instead of guessing a transition name, and where CI moves the
  ticket, do not move it by hand.
- Use the `jira-tickets` skill for the issue-type templates, the area tags, and
  the board rules.

## Task workflow

Every unit of work — a feature, a fix, a refactor, a chore, a documentation
change — follows these steps in order.

1. Analyze the request. Read the code and the existing pattern to reuse before
   the first edit, and resolve ambiguity instead of assuming scope.
2. File the ticket. See the shared ticket rules; investigation writes nothing.
3. Cut the branch, or the ticket worktree where the project uses one, from the
   freshly fetched integration branch.
4. Do the work end to end in that unit: code, tests, docs, migration, SDK
   regeneration, version bump, and changelog entry as the change requires.
5. Commit, push, and open the pull request under the ticket's name. Report the
   PR URL.

Finished work is never left in the working tree or unpushed, and never waits to
be asked for the push.

## Branches, commits, and pull requests

- Never commit to the integration or release branch. Every unit of work gets a
  new branch, cut from the freshly pulled integration branch, named
  `<type>/<scope>-<KEY>-<slug>`. The project's instructions name the branches
  and the key.
- Rebase only a branch you own, at most until review starts, and push the
  rewrite with `--force-with-lease`, never a plain `--force`.
- One logical change per commit, in Conventional Commits:
  `<type>(<scope>): <KEY> <ticket title>`. Types: `build`, `ci`, `docs`, `feat`,
  `fix`, `perf`, `refactor`, `style`, `test`, `chore`, `revert`. What follows
  the key is the ticket's title, not a second sentence written for the commit.
- Every commit is self-contained: it builds and its tests pass on its own. Keep
  generated artefacts in their own commit where the project does.
- One PR per unit of work, opened against the integration branch, titled
  `[<KEY>] <ticket title>`, its body naming the ticket key. A squash merge then
  lands the ticket's own wording.
- Never merge a PR and never enable auto-merge. Merging is the user's job: open
  the PR, report it, and stop.
- After the user merges: remove the ticket worktree, pull the integration
  branch, delete the local and remote branch (`git branch -D`, because a squash
  merge leaves the branch unmerged as far as Git is concerned), and confirm the
  ticket reads `Done`. Never keep working on a merged branch.

## Releases

- A repository that ships carries `release.json` — `{ "version", "name" }` — and
  a `CHANGELOG.md`. Every change a user could notice bumps the version and adds
  its changelog entry under the new version, in the same PR as the code.
- Patch: a fix, and nothing else. Minor: anything else that ships. Major: a
  breaking change to the API or the data model, or a step change in what the
  product is; bump the name too.
- Promote by merge or fast-forward, never by squash, so the release commit
  exists on both branches. Tag `v<version>` on that commit after the promotion
  lands; never tag the integration branch.
- The project's instructions name the commands that verify the version.

## TypeScript

- Never cast a value to silence a type error: no `as SomeType`, `as unknown`,
  `as any`, or `<SomeType>expr`.
- Define the shape before you use it: a `type` alias or an `interface`.
- When a third-party type is too broad, narrow it with a type guard or a
  discriminated union, not a cast.
- Prefer explicit types at module boundaries over inferred return types on
  exported functions.

## Generated code

- Never hand-edit generated output: SDK clients, OpenAPI artefacts, route trees,
  lockfiles, and any file carrying a generation header.
- Change the source, regenerate with the project's task (for example
  `mise run sdk:generate`), then commit the output with the change that caused
  it.
- An API contract change commits the regenerated client in the same PR.

## Database migrations

- Generate migrations through the project's task runner. Never run the ORM's
  generator directly and never hand-write a migration file.
- Always pass an explicit name that describes the schema change, not the
  generator's generated tag.
- Read the generated SQL before committing. Auto-generated statements can drop
  columns or data.
- Migrations are additive: expand and deploy first, contract in a later change,
  so a rollback lands new code on a compatible schema.
- Commit the migration with the schema edit that produced it. The project's
  instructions name the exact commands.

## Secrets

- Secrets come from the project's secret store: Doppler per project and config,
  SOPS with age under `secrets/`, or the platform's own. Never commit a
  plaintext value.
- Never print, log, or paste a decrypted value. Extract one value only when a
  command needs it.
- Never introduce a second secret mechanism without a decision on the ticket.
- A committed `doppler.yaml`, `.sops.yaml`, or tfvars file names identifiers and
  sizing only, never credentials.

## Task runner

- Run repository tasks through mise: `mise run <task>` from the repository root.
  Never call a bare tool binary or a script path when a task exists.
- A missing task is a gap: add it to `mise.toml` with `description`, `dir`,
  `run`, and `depends` where they apply, then use it. Never ship an ad hoc
  command as the deliverable.
- Per-app tasks are `mise run //apps/<app>:<task>`.
- The toolchain comes from `mise install` at the versions pinned in
  `mise.toml`. Bump the pin instead of adding a per-tool install step to CI.

## CI runners

- Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on Blacksmith. Never use
  `ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, `macos-latest`, or a `self-hosted` label.
- Use the smallest runner that fits the job. The default is
  `blacksmith-2vcpu-ubuntu-2404`; then `blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404`,
  `blacksmith-8vcpu-ubuntu-2404`, and `blacksmith-16vcpu-ubuntu-2404`.
- ARM jobs use `blacksmith-<size>vcpu-ubuntu-2404-arm`. macOS jobs use
  `blacksmith-6vcpu-macos-26` or `blacksmith-12vcpu-macos-26`.
- Pin the image in the label. Ubuntu 22.04 tags are deprecated; never use them.
- The Blacksmith GitHub App must be installed on the repository. Without it,
  jobs with a `blacksmith-*` label queue forever. Install it before the first
  workflow change lands.
- Keep the label on the job. Do not set `runs-on` groups, and do not add a
  matrix dimension only to pick a runner size.

## Where documents live

- The repository keeps only what a deploy needs or what derives from the code:
  `docs/adr/` for decisions that ship with the code, `docs/runbook.md` for
  operations, and `docs/architecture.md` for the system as it stands.
- Everything written to be read rather than deployed — an exploration, a design,
  a proposal, a decision write-up, a meeting note — lives in the product's
  Confluence space. Address the space by key; the site holds other products'
  spaces, so never search for it.
- Link both ways: an artefact names its ticket key, and the ticket carries the
  page URL.
- Create and update pages through the `atlassian` MCP server; read and verify
  them with `acli`. See the Confluence page write rule.
- Verify a page with an HTML read, not a markdown one. Dates, panels, and
  decision lists render in Confluence but vanish from a markdown export.
- Use the `confluence-pages` skill for the authoring and verification steps.

## Sentry

- Address an issue by key, `<PROJECT>-<ID>`: the Sentry project slug in upper
  case over the organization that owns both apps. The id is a number or a hex
  string. Never address an issue by URL.
- The organization holds several products, so resolve the key instead of
  searching it.
- A commit that closes an issue carries `Fixes <PROJECT>-<ID>` in its footer.
- Resolve the issue only once the fix is on the branch that deploys it. A
  recurrence before that reopens it as regressed.

## Jira and Confluence access

- Use `acli` for every Atlassian operation except writing a Confluence page. Do
  not call the Atlassian REST API directly, do not authenticate with a
  hand-rolled token, and do not drive the Atlassian web UI.
- Jira: `acli jira workitem view|create|edit|transition`. Read with `--json` and
  name the fields you need.
- Confluence: `acli confluence page view --id <ID> --body-format view`,
  `acli confluence space list`, `acli confluence blog create`.
- Confirm the account before diagnosing a failure: `acli jira auth status`,
  `acli confluence auth status`.
- Prefer `--json` over parsing human-readable tables.
- `acli` missing, unauthenticated, or without the operation you need: stop and
  report exactly what is missing. Do not fall back to a raw API call or the web
  UI. The one exception is creating or updating a Confluence page: `acli` has no
  such command, so that write goes through the Atlassian MCP server, per the
  Confluence page write rule.

## Confluence page writes

`acli` can read a Confluence page but cannot create or update one. That single
operation goes through the `atlassian` MCP server; everything else stays on
`acli`.

- Create with `createConfluencePage`, update with `updateConfluencePage`. Do not
  call the Atlassian REST API directly, do not drive the web UI, and do not
  script the write.
- Load the server's content-format guide for the tool before the first write
  (`getContentFormatGuide`). Build the body in the format the guide names; a
  body assembled without it is usually blank or malformed.
- Address the space by key, and place the page at the space homepage or under
  the page a reader would look in.
- Verify every write afterwards with
  `acli confluence page view --id <ID> --body-format view`. The MCP tool's reply
  confirms the call; the `acli` read confirms the page.
- MCP server unauthenticated or the tool unavailable: stop and report. Never
  substitute the REST API, curl, or the web UI for the write.

## GitHub access

- Use `gh`. Do not call `api.github.com` with curl, do not use a personal
  access token from the environment, and do not drive the GitHub web UI.
- `gh issue`, `gh pr`, `gh run`, and `gh repo` cover the common cases. For an
  endpoint `gh` does not wrap, use `gh api`.
- Prefer `--json` and `--jq` over parsing human-readable tables.
- `gh` missing, unauthenticated, or without the operation you need: stop and
  report exactly what is missing. Do not fall back to a raw API call or the web
  UI.
